introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2025. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 1(a)(i) et (a)(ii) sont regroupées dans la sous-question « a » (5 + 6 = 11 marks imprimés). Calcul numérique du corrigé vérifié : 30 - 9,8 = 20,2 ; 30 - 12 = 18 ; 30 - 5 = 25 (°C). Les gradients adiabatiques (environ 10 et 4 à 9 °C par km) sont des ordres de grandeur classiques.

Question 1(c) : les « deux types climatiques majeurs du Cameroun » sont interprétés comme le climat équatorial du sud et le climat tropical (soudano-sahélien) du nord ; les totaux de pluie et les amplitudes thermiques sont donnés en ordres de grandeur (à faire relire). Le sujet ne nomme pas les deux types.

Page de garde vérifiée : JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, durée Three Hours. Sujet scanné de quatre pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de fond de carte). Filigranes et bandeaux gcerevision.com ignorés.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3 ; Section B : questions 4 à 6 ; Section C : question 7 seule, en deux versions EITHER / OR). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 est codée « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b », « OR-c » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans source consultable. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur. Faits à faire relire par un géographe avant mise en avant. Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment à 25 (Q1 5+6+6+8 ; Q2 8+8+9, la sous-question (a) n'ayant aucun mark imprimé ; Q3 8+9+8 ; Q4 7+8+6+4 ; Q5 6+9+5+5 ; Q6 8+8+9 ; Q7 EITHER 8+8+9, OR 9+8+8). Aucun écart avec le sujet.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) (i) It is raining heavily in one part of your community with thunder and lightning, while in another part the weather is bright with clear skies and abundant sunshine. Using your knowledge of temperature lapse rate, explain the differences in weather conditions between the two parts of your community.

(5 marks)

ii) Show how air masses bring about variations in the type and characteristics of climate across the globe.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Lapse rates and the two kinds of weather (5 marks)**

The **lapse rate** is the rate at which air temperature falls with height. Three rates must be distinguished:

- the **Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR)**: the actual fall of temperature with height in the surrounding air, which varies from place to place and time to time (the average is about 6.5 °C per km);
- the **Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR)**: the cooling of a rising parcel of unsaturated air as it expands, about 10 °C per km (9.8 °C/km);
- the **Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR)**: the cooling of a rising parcel once it is saturated and condensation is taking place; it is smaller (about 4 to 9 °C per km, commonly taken as about 5 °C per km in the tropics) because condensation releases **latent heat**.

A parcel of air rises only as long as it is **warmer (and so less dense) than the surrounding air**; it sinks back when it becomes cooler than its environment. The state of the atmosphere (stable or unstable) therefore depends on the ELR compared with the DALR and the SALR.

**The part with heavy rain, thunder and lightning: unstable air.**
Here the ground is strongly heated (for example bare soil, tarred roads, roofs or a moist area) and the air is humid. The ELR is steep (greater than the DALR, say 12 °C per km). Example: a parcel leaving the ground at 30 °C is at about 20 °C after 1 km (30 - 9.8), while the surrounding air at that height is only 30 - 12 = 18 °C. The parcel is still warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising. It reaches its dew point, condensation begins, a cloud forms and latent heat is released, so it now cools more slowly (at the SALR) and stays warmer than its environment. It continues to rise to great heights and a **cumulonimbus** cloud develops. Ice crystals, water drops and hailstones colliding in the cloud build up electric charges, which produce **lightning and thunder**, and the abundant condensation gives a short, **heavy convectional downpour**. This is the usual afternoon storm of humid tropical regions.

**The part with clear skies and sunshine: stable air.**
Here the ELR is gentle (less than the SALR, say 5 °C per km) or there is a **temperature inversion** (temperature rises with height, for example over a cool shaded area, a lake or a wetland, or in descending air of a high-pressure area). Example: a parcel leaving the ground at 30 °C is at about 20 °C after 1 km, while the surrounding air at that height is 30 - 5 = 25 °C. The parcel is colder and denser than its environment and sinks back to the ground. There is no sustained uplift, no cloud or only a few small fair-weather cumulus, so the sun shines freely.

**Conclusion.** Local differences in surface heating and humidity give different ELR values within the same community; the unstable part has deep convection and storms, while the stable part stays dry and sunny.

**(ii) Air masses and the variations of climate across the globe (6 marks)**

An **air mass** is a very large body of air (often 1000 km or more across) in which the temperature and the humidity are fairly uniform horizontally. It acquires these properties from its **source region** (a large flat surface such as an ocean, a desert or an ice sheet) where it stays for some days. Air masses are classified by latitude (**equatorial, tropical, polar, arctic**) and by surface (**continental**, dry; **maritime**, moist). The main types are:

| Air mass | Source | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical continental (cT) | Sahara and other hot deserts | Hot, very dry, dusty |
| Tropical maritime (mT) | Warm subtropical oceans | Warm, humid, unstable at the surface |
| Equatorial maritime | Equatorial oceans | Hot, very humid |
| Polar continental (cP) | Cold interior of Eurasia and Canada | Very cold and dry in winter |
| Polar maritime (mP) | Cool oceans at high latitudes | Cool, moist and unstable |

**How they cause variations in climate.**

1. **The air mass that dominates a place gives its climate its basic character.** Regions under hot, humid equatorial or tropical maritime air have a hot, wet climate; places under tropical continental air are hot and dry; places under polar continental air have bitterly cold winters.
2. **Seasonal movement of the air masses.** The belts follow the overhead sun, so that many regions are under different air masses at different times of the year, and so have a **seasonal climate**. In West and Central Africa the **Intertropical Convergence (Discontinuity) Zone** separates the moist tropical maritime air (the south-west monsoon from the South Atlantic) from the dry tropical continental air (the north-east trade wind or Harmattan from the Sahara). When the moist air advances north (about April to October) the north of Cameroon has its rainy season; when the dry air returns (November to March) there is a long dry, dusty Harmattan season. The north therefore has one wet season and the equatorial south, which is under maritime air almost all the year, has two. Likewise the monsoon of South Asia brings the moist maritime air in summer and cold dry continental air in winter.
3. **Places where air masses meet.** The boundary between a warm and a cold air mass is a **front**, where the warm air rises over the cold air, giving cloud, rain and changeable weather. This explains the unsettled weather of north-west Europe, which lies where polar maritime and tropical maritime air meet and where depressions are frequent; the climate is moist, mild and changeable. When polar continental air spreads in winter the weather is cold and dry, and when tropical continental air spreads in summer it is hot and dry.
4. **Modification on the move.** An air mass changes as it travels: cold air moving over a warm sea picks up heat and moisture and becomes unstable (showers); warm moist air moving over a cold surface cools and gives fog or drizzle.

**Conclusion.** The kind of air mass, its direction and season of arrival, and where it meets other air masses together explain the type of climate (humid or dry, hot or cold, seasonal or not) in the different parts of the world.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) How do static factors influence the lag time at the gauging station of a drainage basin?

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Terms.** A **drainage basin** is the area drained by a river and its tributaries. At the **gauging station** the discharge of the river is measured, and the **storm hydrograph** plots discharge against time. The **lag time** is the time between the **peak rainfall** and the **peak discharge** at the gauging station. A short lag time gives a steep rising limb and a high, flashy peak (floods are likely); a long lag time gives a gentle, low and flat hydrograph. **Static (fixed) factors** are the permanent characteristics of the basin, which do not change from one storm to the next (unlike the **dynamic** factors such as the intensity and duration of the rainfall, the antecedent soil moisture and the temperature).

**Static factors and their effect on lag time (any three or four, 1.5 to 2 marks each)**

1. **Size of the basin.** In a small basin the rain falls close to the gauging station and runs a short distance, so the lag time is short; in a large basin the water has to travel far and the tributaries peak at different times, so the lag is long.
2. **Shape of the basin.** A **circular** basin brings the water from all the parts of the watershed to the gauging station at about the same time, so the lag time is short and the peak high. An **elongated** basin spreads the arrival of water over a longer time, so the lag is longer and the peak lower.
3. **Relief and slope.** On steep slopes the surface runoff and throughflow move quickly into the channels, so the lag time is short; on gentle slopes the water is slow and has more time to infiltrate, so the lag is long.
4. **Drainage density.** A high drainage density (many streams per square kilometre) means that the water has only a short distance to flow overland before it reaches a channel, so the lag is short; a low density gives a long lag.
5. **Rock type (geology) and soil.** Impermeable rocks and clay soils allow little infiltration, so there is much overland flow and a short lag time. Permeable rocks (sandstone, limestone) and sandy soils absorb water, which flows slowly by throughflow and groundwater flow, so the lag is long and the peak is low.
6. **Land cover and land use (long-term).** Dense vegetation intercepts rain and slows the flow, so the lag is longer; bare ground, and especially **urbanised** areas with concrete, tarred roads and drains, speed the water to the channel, so the lag is shorter and the flood risk is higher. Wetlands and reservoirs in the basin delay the flow.
7. **Channel characteristics.** A short, straight, smooth and steep channel carries the water fast (short lag), while a long, winding and rough channel with a floodplain delays it (long lag).

**Conclusion.** A small, circular, steep, impermeable and urbanised basin with a high drainage density has a short lag time and a flashy hydrograph; a large, elongated, gentle, permeable and well-vegetated basin has a long lag time and a flat one.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) What contrasts exist between the two major climatic types in Cameroon?

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The two major climatic types of Cameroon are the **equatorial (Guinean) climate of the south** and the **tropical (Sudanian and Sahelian) climate of the north**. They are separated by the Adamawa plateau, where there is a transitional (Sudano-Guinean) climate. They differ mainly in the amount and the distribution of the rainfall, which depends on the length of the period during which the moist south-west monsoon (tropical maritime air) blows on the region, as against the dry north-east Harmattan (tropical continental air).

| Aspect | Equatorial climate (south: the forest zone, the Southern Plateau and the coast) | Tropical climate (north: the Benue and the Chad lowlands, Far North) |
|---|---|---|
| **Position** | South of about latitude 6 degrees N | North of the Adamawa plateau, from about 8 degrees N to Lake Chad |
| **Seasons** | Four seasons: a long dry season, a short rainy season, a short dry season and a long rainy season (the pattern is clearest on the plateau, with two rainfall peaks); on the coast the long wet season is much stronger | Two seasons only: a long dry season (about 5 to 8 months, longer towards the north) and a short rainy season (about 4 to 5 months, roughly from May or June to September or October) |
| **Rainfall total** | High, generally 1500 to 2000 mm or more; on the coast and on Mount Cameroon it is much higher (more than 3000 mm at Douala, and among the highest in Africa on the slopes of Mount Cameroon) | Moderate to low, falling from about 1000 mm in the south of the zone to well below 800 mm in the Far North, and the amounts vary a lot from year to year |
| **Rainfall character** | Rain in every month or almost, convectional and relief rain; many rain days; high humidity | Rain falls only in the rainy season, in a few heavy storms and squalls; fewer rain days; low humidity in the dry season |
| **Temperature** | Uniformly warm (annual mean about 24 to 27 °C); small annual range (2 to 3 °C) | Higher means in the extreme north; large annual range (about 6 to 10 °C or more) and large daily range, with very hot days before the rains and cool nights in the Harmattan |
| **Wind and air masses** | Dominated by moist tropical maritime (monsoon) air nearly all the year | Moist monsoon air for a few months only; for most of the year the dry, dusty, north-east Harmattan (tropical continental air) |
| **Vegetation** | Tropical rainforest (dense, evergreen, several layers); mangroves on the coast | Savanna, falling from woodland savanna in the south of the zone to thorn steppe (Sahel) with scattered acacias in the Far North |
| **Effects on land use** | Perennial crops (cocoa, oil palm, rubber, banana, coffee) and root crops (cassava, yam); farming all the year | Cereals (sorghum, millet, maize), cotton, groundnuts, onions and pastoralism; farming restricted to the rainy season, with irrigation (for example, the rice and the dry-season sorghum schemes); risks of drought and desertification |

**Conclusion.** The equatorial south is hot, wet and humid in nearly all the months, whereas the tropical north is hot with a long dry season, scanty and unreliable rainfall and a wide temperature range. These contrasts explain the differences in vegetation, soils, farming and settlement between the two parts of the country.
